parts.label: a
parts.ask: A machine fills packets of sweets and \(\tfrac{1}{7}\) of the packets also contain a prize. There are 40 packets in each box, and \(T\) is the number of packets in a box that contain a prize. State a condition needed for \(T\) to be modelled by \(\mathrm{B}\left(40, \tfrac{1}{7}\right)\).
parts.method: Recall the conditions for a binomial model

steps.text: A binomial model needs independent trials, each with the same probability of success.
steps.why: Answer in context: talk about packets and prizes.

steps.text: Here a trial is one packet, and a success is that packet containing a prize.

parts.answerText: The prizes must be put into packets independently of each other (or: every packet must have the same probability, \(\tfrac{1}{7}\), of containing a prize).

check.answers: a condition for a binomial model, in context: no number to compare

parts.label: b(i)
parts.ask: A box is selected at random. Using \(T \sim \mathrm{B}\left(40, \tfrac{1}{7}\right)\), find the probability that the box has exactly 6 packets containing a prize.
parts.method: State the distribution, then use the binomial formula

steps.why: Or binomial pdf on a calculator: \(n = 40\), \(p = \tfrac{1}{7}\), \(x = 6\).

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.ask: Find the probability that the box has fewer than 3 packets containing a prize.

steps.why: Or binomial cdf on a calculator with \(x = 2\).

parts.label: c
parts.ask: Kamil's sweet shop buys 5 boxes. Find the probability that exactly 2 of these 5 boxes have fewer than 3 packets containing a prize.

steps.text: Let \(K\) be the number of the 5 boxes with fewer than 3 prizes. Each box is one trial, with success probability from (b)(ii).

steps.head: Now the binomial formula with r = 2

answers.derive: binomial(5, 2)*Sum(binomial(40, r)*Rational(1, 7)**r*Rational(6, 7)**(40 - r), (r, 0, 2)).doit()**2*(1 - Sum(binomial(40, r)*Rational(1, 7)**r*Rational(6, 7)**(40 - r), (r, 0, 2)).doit())**3

parts.label: d
parts.ask: Kamil claims that the proportion of packets containing a prize is less than \(\tfrac{1}{7}\). In a random sample of 110 packets, 9 contain a prize. Use a suitable test, at the 5% level of significance, to assess Kamil's claim. State your hypotheses clearly.

steps.why: Kamil says "less than", so the test is one-tailed.

steps.head: The distribution, assuming H0 is true

steps.text: Let \(X\) be the number of packets in the sample that contain a prize.

steps.why: 9 is below this, so we test the lower tail.

steps.head: Probability of a result this extreme

steps.text: The result is significant, so reject \(\mathrm{H}_0\).

parts.answerText: There is evidence at the 5% level to support Kamil's claim that the proportion of packets containing a prize is less than \(\tfrac{1}{7}\).

check.answers: a conclusion in context to a hypothesis test: the probability is checked by assert
check.assert: Abs(N(Sum(binomial(110, r)*Rational(1, 7)**r*Rational(6, 7)**(110 - r), (r, 0, 9)).doit()) - Rational(38292, 1000000)) < Rational(1, 1000000) and N(Sum(binomial(110, r)*Rational(1, 7)**r*Rational(6, 7)**(110 - r), (r, 0, 9)).doit()) < Rational(5, 100)
